easy.text: What is the center of mass of an object?

options.text: The average location of all the mass in an object
options.feedback: Correct -- the center of mass is the balance point where the object's mass is effectively concentrated.

options.text: The heaviest single point on the object
options.feedback: Center of mass is about the overall balance point, not necessarily the single heaviest spot.

options.text: The exact geometric center of any shape, always
options.feedback: For uneven mass distributions, the center of mass can be different from the simple geometric center.

options.text: The point where the object is most colorful
options.feedback: Color has no bearing on the physics concept of center of mass.

medium.text: A hammer has a heavy metal head and a long, light handle. Where is its center of mass most likely located?

options.text: Closer to the heavy metal head
options.feedback: Correct -- center of mass shifts toward the region with more concentrated mass.

options.text: Exactly in the middle of the handle's length
options.feedback: Since the head is much heavier than the handle, the balance point shifts toward the head, not the handle's midpoint.

options.text: At the very tip of the handle, farthest from the head
options.feedback: The heavier head pulls the center of mass toward itself, not away from it.

options.text: Outside the hammer entirely
options.feedback: For a simple, solid object like this, the center of mass is located within the object itself.

hard.text: Why can a tightrope walker balance more easily while holding a long pole horizontally?

options.text: The pole helps keep the overall center of mass lower and more stable, and allows small adjustments to counteract tipping
options.feedback: Correct -- the pole increases rotational inertia and helps shift the combined center of mass to maintain balance.

options.text: The pole eliminates gravity's effect on the walker
options.feedback: Gravity still fully acts on the tightrope walker -- the pole helps manage balance, not eliminate gravity.

options.text: The pole makes the walker weigh less overall
options.feedback: Adding a pole actually increases total weight -- the benefit is about balance and stability, not reducing weight.

options.text: The pole has no actual effect on balance
options.feedback: The pole plays a real, well-understood role in improving balance and stability on the tightrope.

easy.hard: This point represents where an object's mass could be treated as concentrated for analyzing its overall motion.
easy.medium: This is the single point where an object's mass is effectively balanced.
easy.easy: This is the point where an object would balance perfectly if you tried to balance it on your finger.

medium.hard: The balance point shifts toward wherever more mass is concentrated within the object.
medium.medium: The balance point tends to be pulled toward the heavier part of an object.
medium.easy: The heavy metal end pulls the balance point closer to itself.

hard.hard: The pole extends the walker's effective mass distribution, increasing resistance to rotation and allowing fine adjustments that shift the combined center of mass back over the rope.
hard.medium: The pole spreads out mass and lets the walker make small adjustments to keep their overall balance point right over the rope.
hard.easy: The pole helps the walker make small adjustments to keep their balance point centered over the rope.

options.text: The constant maximum speed a falling object reaches when air resistance balances gravity
options.feedback: Correct -- once these two forces balance, the falling object stops accelerating and falls at a steady speed.

options.text: The speed of an object the instant it's dropped
options.feedback: That would just be the initial speed (often zero), not terminal velocity.

options.text: The fastest possible speed anything can ever travel
options.feedback: Terminal velocity is specific to a falling object in a particular fluid, not a universal speed limit.

options.text: The speed at which an object stops falling entirely
options.feedback: The object is still falling at terminal velocity -- it just isn't speeding up anymore.

medium.text: Once an object reaches terminal velocity, what is true about the net force acting on it?

options.text: The net force is zero, since air resistance now equals gravity
options.feedback: Correct -- balanced forces mean no further acceleration, keeping speed constant.

options.text: The net force is at its maximum
options.feedback: Maximum net force would still be accelerating the object -- terminal velocity means forces have balanced out to zero net force.

options.text: Gravity has completely stopped acting on the object
options.feedback: Gravity continues acting the whole time -- it's now balanced by an equal air resistance force, not eliminated.

options.text: Air resistance has dropped to zero
options.feedback: Air resistance is actually at its strongest at terminal velocity, matching gravity's pull exactly.

hard.text: A skydiver falls and eventually reaches terminal velocity. Then they open their parachute. What happens to their speed immediately after opening it, and why?

options.text: Their speed decreases sharply, because the parachute dramatically increases air resistance, making it greater than gravity temporarily
options.feedback: Correct -- the sudden increase in air resistance from the parachute exceeds gravity's pull, causing rapid deceleration until a new, slower terminal velocity is reached.

options.text: Their speed increases sharply
options.feedback: The parachute dramatically increases air resistance, which slows the skydiver down, not speeds them up.

options.text: Their speed stays exactly the same
options.feedback: The parachute significantly changes the balance of forces, causing a noticeable change in speed, not a constant one.

options.text: Gravity briefly stops acting on the skydiver
options.feedback: Gravity continues acting throughout -- what changes is the much larger air resistance force from the parachute.

easy.hard: This describes the point where two opposing forces on a falling object become exactly equal.
easy.medium: This is the top steady speed a falling object reaches once air resistance catches up to gravity.
easy.easy: This is the fastest steady speed something reaches while falling through air.

medium.hard: At this state, the upward and downward forces on the object cancel out exactly, resulting in zero net force.
medium.medium: At this point, the upward push of air resistance exactly cancels gravity's downward pull.
medium.easy: At this point, air resistance pushing up exactly balances gravity pulling down.

hard.hard: The sudden large increase in air resistance temporarily exceeds gravity's pull, creating a net upward force that rapidly decelerates the skydiver until a new balance point (slower terminal velocity) is reached.
hard.medium: The parachute suddenly creates a lot more air resistance than gravity can match, so the skydiver quickly slows down.
hard.easy: The parachute creates so much more air resistance than gravity that the skydiver quickly slows down.

easy.text: What does voltage measure in an electrical circuit?

options.text: The difference in electric potential energy between two points
options.feedback: Correct -- voltage is essentially the 'push' that drives current through a circuit.

options.text: The total amount of charge stored in a battery
options.feedback: That's closer to a description of capacity/charge, not voltage specifically.

options.text: The physical size of a wire
options.feedback: Wire size relates to resistance and current capacity, not voltage directly.

options.text: The color of the electrical current
options.feedback: Electric current doesn't have a color -- this isn't a meaningful description of voltage.

medium.text: A 9V battery and a 1.5V battery are both connected to identical circuits. Which one will generally push more current through, assuming the same resistance?

options.text: The 9V battery, since higher voltage drives more current through the same resistance
options.feedback: Correct -- by Ohm's law (I=V/R), a higher voltage with the same resistance results in more current.

options.text: The 1.5V battery
options.feedback: Lower voltage would drive less current through the same resistance, not more.

options.text: Both will push exactly the same current
options.feedback: With different voltage values and the same resistance, the resulting current should differ.

options.text: Neither battery can push any current at all
options.feedback: Both batteries can drive current through a completed circuit -- the difference is in how much current flows.

hard.text: Voltage is often compared to water pressure in a pipe analogy. In this analogy, what does current correspond to, and what does resistance correspond to?

options.text: Current corresponds to the flow rate of water; resistance corresponds to how narrow or obstructed the pipe is
options.feedback: Correct -- higher pressure (voltage) with less pipe obstruction (resistance) results in a greater flow rate (current).

options.text: Current corresponds to the water's temperature; resistance corresponds to the color of the pipe
options.feedback: Temperature and color aren't meaningful analogies in this framework -- flow rate and pipe narrowness are the standard comparisons.

options.text: Current corresponds to the pipe's length; resistance corresponds to the water's taste
options.feedback: These aren't the standard mappings used in the water-pressure analogy for electricity.

options.text: Current and resistance both correspond to the same thing: water pressure
options.feedback: Current and resistance represent two distinct concepts in the analogy -- flow rate and pipe restriction, respectively -- not the same thing.

easy.hard: This quantity represents the 'push' or potential energy difference that drives charge to move.
easy.medium: This is the electrical 'push' that makes current flow through a circuit.
easy.easy: This is what pushes electric current through a wire, like pressure pushes water through a pipe.

medium.hard: According to Ohm's law, current is directly proportional to voltage when resistance is held constant.
medium.medium: A bigger 'push' (higher voltage) results in more current flowing, if resistance stays the same.
medium.easy: A bigger battery voltage pushes more current through, if the resistance is the same.

hard.hard: In this analogy, pressure maps to voltage, flow rate maps to current, and pipe restriction/narrowness maps to resistance.
hard.medium: Current is like how fast the water flows, and resistance is like how narrow or blocked the pipe is.
hard.easy: Current is like the water's flow speed, and resistance is like how narrow the pipe is.

easy.text: What shape is a concave mirror?

options.text: Curved inward, like the inside of a bowl
options.feedback: Correct -- a concave mirror's reflective surface curves inward.

options.text: Curved outward, like the outside of a ball
options.feedback: That describes a convex mirror, the opposite curvature.

options.text: Perfectly flat
options.feedback: A flat mirror is neither concave nor convex -- it's a plane mirror.

options.text: Shaped like a cube
options.feedback: Mirrors used for these optical effects are curved, not cube-shaped.

medium.text: Why are convex mirrors commonly used as side mirrors on cars?

options.text: They provide a wider field of view, helping drivers see more of what's behind and beside them
options.feedback: Correct -- convex mirrors spread out the reflected image, showing a broader area than a flat mirror would.

options.text: They make objects appear closer than they actually are
options.feedback: Convex mirrors actually make objects appear farther away/smaller than they really are, which is the opposite effect (this is why they include a 'objects are closer than they appear' warning).

options.text: They completely block glare from other headlights
options.feedback: Glare reduction isn't the primary reason for using a convex shape -- their wide field of view is the key benefit.

options.text: They are cheaper to manufacture than flat mirrors
options.feedback: Cost isn't the functional reason for choosing a convex shape -- the wider viewing angle is the practical benefit.

hard.text: A concave mirror can form either a real, inverted image or a virtual, upright image, depending on conditions. What determines which type of image forms?

options.text: Whether the object is placed farther than or closer than the mirror's focal point
options.feedback: Correct -- objects beyond the focal point produce real, inverted images, while objects within the focal point produce virtual, upright, magnified images.

options.text: The color of the object being reflected
options.feedback: Color doesn't determine the type of image formed -- object distance relative to the focal point does.

options.text: The time of day the mirror is used
options.feedback: Time of day has no effect on the optical image-forming properties of a mirror.

options.text: Whether the mirror is being cleaned or not
options.feedback: Cleanliness doesn't affect the fundamental optical behavior determining image type -- object distance from the focal point does.

easy.hard: This mirror's surface curves toward the direction the viewer is looking from.
easy.medium: This mirror curves inward, like the inside of a spoon.
easy.easy: This mirror curves inward, like the inside of a spoon.

medium.hard: This mirror's outward curve spreads reflected light rays apart, effectively capturing a broader visual area in the same mirror size.
medium.medium: This mirror's curve spreads out the reflection, letting the driver see a wider area behind the car.
medium.easy: This mirror's curved shape lets drivers see a wider area behind the car.

hard.hard: The critical dividing line is the mirror's focal point -- object position relative to that point determines whether light rays converge to form a real image or appear to diverge from behind the mirror as a virtual image.
hard.medium: It depends on whether the object is farther away than or closer than a specific key distance from the mirror, called the focal point.
hard.easy: It depends on whether the object is farther or closer than a specific distance from the mirror called the focal point.

options.text: A force that causes an object to rotate around a pivot point
options.feedback: Correct -- torque is the rotational equivalent of a regular pushing or pulling force.

options.text: The total distance an object travels
options.feedback: Distance traveled is unrelated to torque, which is specifically about rotational force.

options.text: The temperature of a rotating object
options.feedback: Temperature has no direct relationship to torque.

options.text: The color of a spinning wheel
options.feedback: Color has no bearing on the physics concept of torque.

medium.text: Why is it easier to loosen a tight bolt using a longer wrench rather than a shorter one?

options.text: A longer wrench increases the torque produced by the same applied force, since torque depends on distance from the pivot
options.feedback: Correct -- torque equals force times the distance from the pivot point, so a longer wrench multiplies the effect of the same push.

options.text: A longer wrench makes the bolt physically smaller
options.feedback: The wrench's length doesn't change the bolt's size -- it changes how much rotational force (torque) you can generate.

options.text: A longer wrench weighs less, making it easier to use
options.feedback: Weight of the wrench isn't the reason for the mechanical advantage -- it's the increased leverage distance.

options.text: There is no actual advantage to using a longer wrench
options.feedback: Using a longer wrench genuinely does provide more torque for the same applied force -- this is a well-established mechanical principle.

hard.text: A force of 20 N is applied perpendicular to a wrench at a distance of 0.3 meters from the bolt. What is the resulting torque?

options.text: 6 N·m
options.feedback: Correct -- torque equals force times distance: 20×0.3=6.
This adds the values instead of multiplying force by distance.
This divides instead of multiplying force by distance.
This doesn't match multiplying 20 by 0.3 correctly.

easy.hard: This quantity results from a force applied at some distance from a pivot point, causing rotation.
easy.medium: This is the rotational push or twist you apply, like when turning a wrench or a doorknob.
easy.easy: This is the twisting force you apply, like when you turn a wrench.

medium.hard: This quantity depends on both the applied force AND the distance from the pivot at which it's applied.
medium.medium: A wrench's length acts like a lever, multiplying the twisting effect of the same push.
medium.easy: A longer wrench gives you more twisting power for the same amount of push.

hard.hard: Multiply the applied force by the perpendicular distance from the pivot point to compute torque.
hard.medium: Multiply the force value by the distance value.
hard.easy: Multiply 20 by 0.3 to find the torque.
